content.title: About
content.content: Beef is the meat of cattle, obtained from various parts of the carcass. Round steak comes from the rear section of the animal and is a lean cut with a mild flavor and moderate fat. It is commonly grilled, pan‑seared, or roasted to retain juiciness and aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The round cut is located in the hindquarter and is one of the leanest beef cuts.
Beef is a rich source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.
Historically, round steak has been used in high‑cuisine dishes such as steak tartare and beef carpaccio.
Meat quality depends heavily on cattle breed, rearing conditions, and aging process.
In some regions the round is also called “top‑blade” or “bottom round.”

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Beef provides all essential amino acids needed for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Heme iron from beef helps prevent anemia, especially in women and children.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals boost immunity and aid wound healing.

items.title: Creatine
items.content: Natural creatine in beef enhances muscular energy metabolism, beneficial for athletes.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Excessive intake may raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: Undercooked beef can harbor pathogens such as E. coli and Salmonella.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef proteins.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: High amounts can exacerbate gout symptoms.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Round steak is best cooked to medium‑rare (55‑60 °C) to keep it tender. Marinate in olive oil with herbs, sear on a hot pan, or grill. Slice thinly and serve with vegetables, sauces, or in salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh beef in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C, wrapped in plastic film or in an airtight container. For longer storage freeze at –18 °C using vacuum‑sealed bags. Thaw frozen beef in the fridge, not at room temperature, before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned clams are a seafood product made from fresh clams that are cleaned, cooked, and sealed in an airtight jar with brine or sauce. They retain a delicate marine flavor, a faint sweetness, and a tender yet firm texture. The product is ready to eat straight from the can.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Clams are bivalve mollusks and have been harvested by humans for thousands of years.
Canning extends the shelf life of clams up to three years while preserving most of their nutrients.
Canned clams are sold in brine, oil, or tomato sauce, each giving a distinct taste profile.
Clams are rich in iron, zinc, and vitamin B12, making them a valuable addition for pescatarians.
In many cultures clams are considered a delicacy and are served as appetizers with sparkling wine.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Canned clams provide about 12 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: They contain notable amounts of iron, zinc, and selenium, essential for immune function and metabolism.

items.title: Vitamin B12 source
items.content: Vitamin B12 is crucial for nervous system health and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Canned clams typically have less than 2 g of fat per 100 g, suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: They provide EPA and DHA, which support heart and brain health.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to clams.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Canned clams often contain a lot of salt; people with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Possible toxins
items.content: If harvested from polluted waters, clams may contain heavy metals or biotoxins.

items.title: Bacterial growth after opening
items.content: Once opened, store the clams in the refrigerator and consume within 1–2 days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned clams can be eaten straight from the jar, added to salads, pasta, rice dishes, or soups. They are also used in stuffing for pies and as a topping for toast. For extra flavor, briefly sauté clams with garlic and herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, transfer clams to an airtight container and refrigerate, using them within 2 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Cranberries (Vaccinium macrocarpon) are small, round, bright red, very tart berries native to North America. They grow on low vines in bogs and are rarely eaten raw because of their sharp sourness. Cranberries are most often eaten dried and sweetened, or as juice, sauce, and in baked goods, and are a traditional food at holiday meals in North America.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cranberries are harvested by flooding the bogs, so the floating berries can be gathered.
The berries bounce when ripe, and air pockets inside them make them float.
Cranberries are very tart because of their acids and low sugar content, so most products are sweetened.
They contain proanthocyanidins, plant compounds studied for urinary tract health.
Cranberries are related to blueberries.

items.title: Rich in polyphenols
items.content: Cranberries contain proanthocyanidins and other polyphenols with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Provides vitamin C
items.content: Fresh cranberries provide vitamin C, which supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Cranberries contribute fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: Provides manganese
items.content: Manganese supports normal metabolism and bone health.

items.title: May support urinary tract health
items.content: Some studies suggest cranberry products may help reduce the risk of recurring urinary tract infections in some people, but they are not a treatment.

items.title: Added sugar
items.content: Dried cranberries, juice cocktails, and sauces usually contain a lot of added sugar, so check labels.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidity of cranberries may cause heartburn or irritate sensitive stomachs and teeth.

items.title: Kidney stones
items.content: Cranberries contain oxalates, which people prone to kidney stones may need to limit.

items.title: Possible medication interactions
items.content: Large amounts of cranberry juice or supplements may interact with blood thinners such as warfarin. People taking prescription drugs should consult a healthcare professional.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fresh cranberries can be cooked into sauces, relishes, and compotes with sweetener, baked into muffins, breads, and desserts, or blended into smoothies. Dried cranberries can be added to oatmeal, salads, granola, and trail mix in small amounts. Choose unsweetened or low-sugar products when possible.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh cranberries in the refrigerator, where they keep for several weeks, or freeze them for up to a year. Dried cranberries keep for several months in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Discard soft, shriveled, or moldy berries.

content.title: About
content.content: Green bean casserole is a classic American side dish made with canned green beans, a creamy mushroom sauce, and crispy fried onions. It is especially popular during holiday meals such as Thanksgiving.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish was created in the 1950s after Campbell’s introduced a ready‑made mushroom sauce.
The original recipe uses a fried onion topping that is added at the end of baking for crunch.
Green bean casserole is considered an iconic part of the American fall table.
Variations include adding cheese, bacon, or nuts for extra flavor.
It scales easily, making it a favorite for large gatherings.

items.title: Rich in vegetables
items.content: Green beans provide vitamins A, C, K, folate, and dietary fiber that support digestive health.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: A typical serving contains about 150‑200 kcal, making it a moderately low‑calorie side.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Phytonutrients in the beans help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Fiber and potassium contribute to healthy blood pressure.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Green beans add a modest amount of protein, useful for vegetarians.

items.title: Mushroom allergy
items.content: The mushroom sauce can trigger reactions in people allergic to mushrooms.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauce often contains a lot of salt; low‑sodium versions are recommended.

items.title: Added sugar in canned beans
items.content: Some canned beans have added sugars; choose unsweetened varieties.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: High fiber may cause gas or bloating in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the casserole hot as a side dish or part of a main course. Bake until the onion topping is golden, or reheat in the microwave. It pairs well with turkey, chicken, or as a vegetarian centerpiece.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze up to 2 months; reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Infant formula for premature babies, ready‑to‑feed, is designed for newborns born before 37 weeks of gestation. It provides higher levels of protein, fat, vitamins and minerals needed for accelerated growth and organ development.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The formula is specifically formulated for infants born before the 37th week of pregnancy.
Ready‑to‑feed format eliminates the need for sterilization or reconstitution.
Contains DHA and ARA to support brain and visual development in preterm infants.
Often includes prebiotics that promote a healthy gut microbiome.
Commonly used in neonatal intensive care units as part of standard feeding protocols.

items.title: Supports growth
items.content: Increased protein and energy content helps premature infants gain weight and length at a faster rate.

items.title: Brain development
items.content: Added DHA and ARA aid in the formation of neural connections and visual function.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamins A, C, E and zinc contribute to the development of the infant’s immune defenses.

items.title: Gut health
items.content: Prebiotics and moderate enzyme levels support a balanced microbiota and reduce intolerance risk.

items.title: Reduces anemia risk
items.content: Readily absorbable iron helps prevent iron‑deficiency anemia in preterm babies.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some newborns may develop an allergy to casein or whey proteins.

items.title: Fluid overload
items.content: Excessive intake can lead to hypernatremia in infants with immature kidneys.

items.title: Improper storage
items.content: After opening, the formula must be refrigerated and used within 24 hours.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Certain formulas contain higher lactose levels, requiring monitoring in infants with lactase deficiency.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: The formula is poured directly from the ready‑to‑feed container into a sterile nipple or bottle. Check the expiration date and package integrity before first use. Consult a neonatologist if you have any doubts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened containers in a cool, dry place away from direct light. Once opened, keep refrigerated and use within 24 hours. Discard if the product develops an off‑odor, discoloration, or abnormal texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Pig in a blanket are bite‑size snacks consisting of small sausages wrapped in flaky or yeasted dough. They are commonly served hot as an appetizer, bar snack, or part of a festive spread. The “1818” version refers to the classic recipe popular in the United States and the United Kingdom.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in the United States in the early 20th century as quick street food.
The name comes from the resemblance of the finished product to a tiny pig wrapped in a “blanket” of dough.
In the UK a similar snack is called a “corn‑wurst” where a sausage is wrapped in a simple flour‑water dough.
There are many dough variations: puff pastry, yeasted dough, wheat‑based, or gluten‑free.
In the US they are often served with mustard, ketchup, or honey‑mustard dipping sauce.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: The sausage provides animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: Combined dough and meat give a quick source of calories useful during high physical activity.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and yeasted dough are rich in B1, B2, and B12 vitamins, supporting nervous system function.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Sausages supply iron, important for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Calcium (when using milk‑based dough)
items.content: Dough made with milk adds calcium, beneficial for bone health.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Sausages often contain a lot of salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Fatty sausage varieties increase saturated fat intake.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional dough contains wheat; people with celiac disease need a gluten‑free version.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Some sausages contain nitrites and other preservatives that should be limited.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pig in a blanket are usually baked in the oven or pan‑fried until golden brown, then served hot with mustard, ketchup, cheese sauce, or honey‑mustard dip. They pair well with fresh vegetables or a simple salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked pieces in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Frozen portions keep for up to 2 months; reheat at 180 °C until crisp. Do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Whiskey sour is a classic cocktail made with whiskey, fresh lemon juice, and simple syrup. Sometimes an egg white is added for a silky foam. The drink balances acidity, sweetness, and the woody notes of the whiskey.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first recorded Whiskey sour recipe appeared in 1862 in "The Bartender's Guide".
It is one of the five "essential" cocktails (Old Fashioned, Martini, Manhattan, Daiquiri, Whiskey Sour) listed in the 1930s "Savoy Cocktail Book".
The original recipe called for American bourbon, though rye whiskey is also common today.
Egg white (the "float") is added to soften the acidity and create a smooth foam.
The drink’s popularity surged in the 2020s as craft bartenders experiment with fruit and spice variations.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Lemon juice is rich in vitamin C, which helps combat free radicals.

items.title: Moderate alcohol content
items.content: Moderate whiskey consumption may support cardiovascular health thanks to its polyphenols.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: The acidity of lemon stimulates gastric juice production, aiding digestion.

items.title: Alcohol
items.content: Excessive alcohol intake leads to health deterioration, dependence, and increased injury risk.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High amounts of lemon juice can irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: If egg white is used, individuals with egg allergy may experience reactions.

content.title: How to Make
content.content: Combine 45 ml bourbon, 30 ml fresh lemon juice, and 15 ml simple syrup in a shaker with ice. Optionally add 15 ml egg white. Shake vigorously for 10–12 seconds, then strain into a glass over fresh ice. Garnish with a maraschino cherry or a lemon wedge.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store ingredients separately: whiskey in a cool, dark place; lemons in the refrigerator; simple syrup in a sealed bottle in the fridge for up to a week. Use egg white immediately after separating.
